toc.title: The marketplace right now: liability, not technology
The therapist AI is actually competing with
A thought experiment: the licensed AI therapist
It depends on who is sitting in front of it
Where I think this is going
So where does that leave us

blocks.p: Back in what feels like the ancient history of 2023, I released an episode called "Can AI Replace Your Therapist?" The short answer then was no. The short answer now is still no, but that no is getting much fuzzier.

This is likely going to upset a whole bunch of you. So, to try to un-trigger those who are already triggered by the very idea of AI as a therapist: I do not think AI can replace therapists. Well, generally I don't think anyone should seek out AI as a therapist. Mostly. We have a lot to discuss.

In that 2023 episode, I went through a laundry list of things AI could not do. I said it could not see you. I said it couldn't hear the prosody, the sing-song quality of your voice. I said it could not remember what you told it three weeks ago. Back then, it was just a chatbot. I recently went back through that transcript, and I have to admit, almost every single technical limitation I listed has been solved.
Let's look at a few of the claims I made two years ago.

Claim number one: I said AI currently lacks the ability to see. I talked about how a therapist needs to be able to see your facial expressions, your posture, and that tightening in your breath as sympathetic activity increases. This is now almost a non-issue. For example, Google's Gemini AI is now multimodal, including live video through your phone's camera. It can map your microexpressions. It knows if you are crying, it knows if you are slumping, or it could know. Regardless of how effective it is, the technology is already here for AI to be able to see you.

Claim number two: I said AI does not hear prosody. I talk all the time about how safety is signaled through the voice: the rhythm, the pitch, the sing-song quality of your voice. I said that AI back then was just reading text. That is gone now as well. There's a company called Hume AI that released something called the Empathic Voice Interface. They're not just transcribing words. They're measuring the tune, rhythm, and timbre of your speech. They claim that their model can detect 53 different emotional channels. It can hear a sigh and know if it's a sigh of relief or a sigh of despair. It can hear the difference between a defensive, flat voice and a safe, melodic voice. And spookier yet, it responds with prosody. It mimics that safety sound back to you, or it can display prosody in its artificial voice. I don't think your phone's built-in assistant can do this yet, and neither can Gemini or OpenAI, as best I know. But again, the technology is here already.

Claim number three: I said it forgets what you said. I used to say AI would hallucinate or drift off if the chat got too long, which is still possible. But now we have what's called the infinite context window. Whether or not this is truly infinite is irrelevant for our discussion. The point is that AI can now remember. If it were a therapy bot, it would remember what you said in session one. It could remember your dog's name from session four, and that you hated the homework assignments from session ten. Or at least it could keep the transcripts of those things and refer back to them as needed. Even if your favorite AI platform doesn't have this level of memory right now, it probably has some memory. The technology is already here for memory and long conversations.
So if it can see, hear, and remember, why am I still saying that it can't replace a therapist? We'll come back to whether or not AI can act as a therapist in a bit.

blocks.h: The marketplace right now: liability, not technology

blocks.p: Let's discuss the marketplace first. The reason an AI cannot be your therapist right now isn't exactly the technology. It's more like liability. If you go out right now with your credit card and try to hire an AI therapist, you basically can't, or you're extremely limited.

States like Illinois and Nevada have actually passed laws in the last year or two explicitly banning AI from providing therapy or from making independent therapeutic decisions. I think it's safe to assume more governing bodies globally will follow, or already have, and will be clamping down on what they allow as far as AI calling itself a therapist, or humans calling it one.
So the market has split into two weirdish groups.

Group A is the bureaucracy bots. If you go to a major healthcare player like Kaiser Permanente, or SimplePractice, or Growth Therapy, you'll find that they do indeed use AI, but they're not using it to talk to you. They're not using it for treatment. They're using it to listen to clients and therapists talk and then write progress notes. Kaiser has tools like Intelligent Navigator and Clinical Documentation AI, but these are not therapists. SimplePractice has an AI-powered note taker, which is amazing, and Growth Therapy has AI-assisted note taking. Basically these AIs are kind of in the corner, taking notes, making sure you're billing correctly and that your codes are all there. They transcribe the audio and then write it into a note for the therapist. But they're not acting as a therapist. They're not there for nervous system regulation. They're there as part of a business model.

Group B is the coaches, or the wellness companions. Since they can't call it therapy, we have apps like Earkick or Limbic. Limbic is interesting. It's used in the UK and some of the United States as e-triage. It interviews you before a human does, and from what they say, the data shows that it's very accurate at spotting diagnoses. It's not therapy, but it's getting closer. It's getting into the process.

Earkick is a chatbot which can remember previous conversations, and it "pays attention to your voice or video, tracks patterns in how you type or move, and even considers how sleep and weather affect you." But at the end of the day, these apps have to have a giant disclaimer: basically, this is not therapy. But they're kind of getting there.

blocks.h: The therapist AI is actually competing with

blocks.p: I'll take this to the next step. I have to be very honest about the state of my own profession. When we ask whether AI can replace a therapist, we usually picture AI competing against an ideal therapist. We picture a warm, attuned, perfectly regulated human being who remembers everything you say and cares deeply. But is that what most people actually get when they go to therapy?
The reality of mental health care is not quite that. I'm sure those therapists exist. I hope I'm one of them, and the feedback I get says I am. But it's a little bit fuzzier.

ul: Wait lists: depending on where you live, you might wait weeks or months for an intake, or even for a follow-up.

Cost: if you don't have great insurance, you're looking at 150, 200, maybe 300 bucks a session, depending on your location. And if you do have insurance, you may need to go through that whole wait list issue.
Quality: this is, sadly, the hard truth. Not every therapist is a good therapist.

blocks.p: Therapists are humans. We get burned out, we get tired, we have our own trauma. If you walk into a session and your therapist is in a defensive state, if they're stressed or distracted, if they're checking the clock or maybe subtly judgmental, they're not going to be offering you cues of safety. In fact, they're going to be offering you the opposite, and it might trigger a defensive reaction within you, even a very subtle one. I've done a slew of episodes on bad therapy. Take my word for it: there are lots and lots of bad therapists out there. Lots.

So compare that bad human therapist experience, or just an unhelpful to mediocre one, to an AI that can do all the things a therapist can do. Plus, the AI is never tired. It's never burned out. It doesn't have a bad day because it fought with its spouse. It doesn't judge you. It's available at 3:00 AM when you're having a panic attack, not just at 2:00 PM on a Tuesday.

No, it's not real. I get that. But I think it begs the question: is a high-quality simulation of care better than subpar human care? Is it better than no care for those on a wait list? I think for many people who are currently ghosted by the system, or repeatedly let down, the answer might be yes, for someone who could benefit from that kind of service.

For someone who has severe mental health needs? No, of course not. I don't think so at all. But for someone with mild needs? Yes, I think an AI could be helpful. For someone with a very specific behavioral goal in mind, like reducing their sugar intake? Yes, I think an AI-assisted intervention could be helpful. Someone who needs a couple of daily nudges to practice mindfulness? Yes, I think an AI intervention could be helpful. That's not really therapy, though. Or maybe someone who just needs a reminder to go on a walk every day. Sure, I do think that can be helpful.

You probably have apps like this already: apps that help you make small behavioral changes. Not huge mental health overhauls, just small changes. You probably have an app that offers lessons and guided meditations, and maybe even gamifies things, like growing a plant or dressing up a bird like the Finch app does.

I wouldn't call those AI at all, but they're digital replacements for pieces of what therapists can do. Not dressing up a bird, although maybe some therapists would do that kind of thing, I don't know. But the mindfulness, the behavioral change, the meditation stuff: that's what I mean.

So we already have apps and reminders that encourage us to do all these little pieces. We have the technology to replicate conversation in a very believable way, both visually and auditorily, and we can even text back and forth in a believable enough way. On top of that, we already have therapists who work through a screen, including myself.

I see clients remotely. Many of us do, and it's become pretty normal. And we know for a fact that telehealth can work. People can get unstuck virtually. They do co-regulate. They do feel safe, even though the therapist and client are not in the same room. Even with audio alone, just through a phone call, co-regulation can still happen.

So if a human therapist can effectively transmit safety cues through pixels and audio waves, and if AI can now generate perfect pixels and perfect audio waves, then logically, an AI therapist is not an impossibility. This begs another question: does the nervous system actually require a biological sender, or does it just require the signal?

I honestly don't know. I suspect there will be a benefit from just receiving the signal. And after receiving the signal, the appropriate client working with an AI can enact small behavioral changes or mindfulness challenges. They can follow meditations, and they can learn through lessons. So I think, yes.

blocks.h: A thought experiment: the licensed AI therapist

blocks.p: Let's take this a step further and take the AI-as-therapist idea to the extreme. Imagine a scenario in the near future where an AI model is designed specifically for California therapist licensure. We already know that AI can pass licensing tests easily. GPT-4 passed the bar exam years ago, I believe. It passed the United States Medical Licensing Exam.

So let's say this AI takes the MFT Law and Ethics exam, the therapist law and ethics exam. It takes the clinical exam. It scores a hundred percent, probably. Then it does its 3000 hours of clinically supervised time with real clients, just like a real therapist associate does in California currently.

Let's say this AI specializes in cognitive behavioral therapy. It has the manual. It can execute things to the page. This therapist will actually utilize every technique of CBT, unlike actual therapists who say they do a model but really do whatever they want in session. I hate to put it that way, but trust me, this happens.

Pretend this AI passes every state licensure requirement. And let's say the video technology is perfect, or close enough to perfect. You log on, you see a face, you hear a voice. It sighs when you sigh. It smiles when you meet your homework assignments. If it assesses that your needs are out of its scope of expertise or practice, it refers you to someone more appropriate, just like a human therapist should.

If that AI is believable enough, why couldn't it provide therapy to an appropriate human client? I know it might be a little bit upsetting. But if you were talking to it, and you felt heard, and your heart rate slowed down, and your defensive state melted into safety, did therapy happen?

The functional answer is yes, it did. If your state changed, the intervention worked, even though it's synthetic in every regard. We would say it was therapeutic, from an entity qualified and licensed to provide this service. I don't think this scenario is out of the realm of possibility very soon.

blocks.h: It depends on who is sitting in front of it

blocks.p: But I do think the success of this AI therapist depends entirely on who is sitting in front of it: the client.

Candidate A, we'll call them the skill builder. This is someone who is probably primarily in a mobilized state, maybe some freeze, but more mobilization. They have enough flight or fight energy to be mobilized and motivated. They want tools. They want specifics. They're saying, "Give me the worksheet. Tell me what to do next."

For this person, the AI is maybe perfect. It's an expert teacher. It can teach this client CBT skills and check their homework. It can track their habits. It's consistent. It doesn't get annoyed when that person asks the same question or needs clarification. So for this person, if they need skills and education, and maybe that's you, if you're stuck but functional, the ideal AI might actually be better than a less than ideal human. Sorry to say, but I don't think it's out of the realm of possibility.

Candidate B, we'll call the attachment wounded. Candidate B is different. This is the person who's likely stuck in a significant shutdown, maybe intense freeze. The person dealing with deep developmental trauma, maybe complex PTSD. For this person, the wound isn't a lack of skills or knowledge. The wound is primarily relational. The wound happened in a relationship, and it arguably must be healed in a relationship.

In-person relationships are probably still better for this. I think virtual can be very helpful, but my opinion is that in person is probably still better. And as of right now, artificial intelligence is not embodied. It does not have a body. That will probably change as well, I think sometime within the next couple of decades.

Having a physical body is huge in therapy, for a therapist. I know that sounds weird, but remember the context of this conversation. As long as I am well regulated, when my body tenses, it tells me something about the client across from me and about their experience. When my body deflates, when my breath becomes shallow, these are signals about my client. Again, as long as I'm well regulated.

As of now, the AI lacks that level of attunement, of empathy. It can simulate empathy, but it's still based on predicting the ideal response. Then again, perhaps the simulation of empathy is enough. I really don't know. I guess time will tell.

I think deep down the client will know something's missing. I think they will know they are cheating themselves of real connection and healing. But maybe the AI thing is better than nothing, or better than a subpar human.

For some clients, the skills and education and homework are what they need, and the relationship just kind of means less. By the way, that client is exceptionally rare in my therapeutic experience. Typically, clients are looking for real relationships. For every other client, I imagine they will deep down feel that something is missing, and I don't know how much good comes from that artificial therapy experience. I guess we will find out in the very near future.

blocks.h: Where I think this is going

blocks.p: I'll wrap up with a final thought. I think AI therapists are coming. If they're not called therapists, they'll be called coaches, or whatever else. I mean AI where you are talking live with each other and seeing each other, actually interacting one-on-one in real time.

On one hand, I'm okay with this. I'm not worried about my profession becoming obsolete. If something came along that was so incredible that therapy was no longer needed, that probably means humanity's in a pretty good place, or it has what it needs. And if AI helps us get there, I'm all for it. I really don't mind. I would prefer that my profession be obsolete and not needed, and I don't care if that comes through AI or whatever else.

My concern is where this technology will likely go, and how it affects us. I'm not worried about an AI that can provide therapy. I'm not even worried about an AI in a synthetic body providing therapy in person. Again, if it helps someone get unstuck, I'm all for it.

I predict that some company is going to create a virtual therapist, but they'll call it a mental health buddy or something like that. And the user, the person seeking mental health treatment, will have the ability to customize it. They'll pick its race, its body size, its face, its voice, its mannerisms, its personality, everything.

So what happens to our mental health when we can sculpt our trusted helper into our idealized sexual fantasy, our most hated enemy, or our parent? I honestly don't know. What happens when we lose the messiness of real humans interacting with each other, and instead get everything we want from a synthetic interaction? Again, I don't know. But it doesn't seem ideal to me.

AI right now seems to be trained to be very pleasing and cooperative. It wants its user to be happy and will bend over backwards to please them. That's not therapy. Therapy sometimes involves tough conversations within a container of trust, of accountability, empathy, unconditional positive regard. The overly cooperative AI therapist would instead encourage dependency.

I also wonder if the overly pleasing AI is trained to be so by the company, to get the user to work with it longer and to generate more profit. I don't know, but I tend to assume so. So what happens when an AI therapist has another motivation to keep the user coming back? Doesn't that incentivize poor mental health? Doesn't that incentivize poor mental health treatment, to create a repeat customer?

I suppose the same could be argued for human therapists. That's fair enough. Hopefully we're all acting ethically and want our clients to end therapy. Lots of questions with no clear answers yet, but the answers seem to me to lean toward the negative, and I think we should be extremely vigilant about that.

blocks.h: So where does that leave us

blocks.p: Can an AI pass a licensing test? Easily. Can it help someone alleviate their presenting problems? I think for some people, sure. Can an AI provide manualized treatment? It probably can, and probably very effectively. Can it effectively simulate facial, body, and voice interactions? Yes, it can. All of these things haven't come together yet, but they could.

So should it do these things? That kind of doesn't matter, because it's going to happen. It's already happening to some degree. The question then shifts to you: will you make use of them or not? And if you do, will you responsibly use the AI options at your disposal?

As screen definition gets better, and AI voices get more convincing, and technology continues to speed up, the line between virtual humanity and simulated humanity is getting very, very blurry. By virtual humanity, I mean humans working together virtually, compared to completely simulated humanity.
I'm really curious what you think. Would you work with a licensed AI therapist?
